headline: Static Check Script Catches 8 Automation Defects in 1 Second
summary: A new Node.js script uses the TypeScript compiler to find selector drift before tests even run, drastically cutting down debugging time.
details: End-to-end (E2E) tests can be time-consuming, often failing due to simple selector mismatches that take hours to diagnose. This new script offers a solution by performing a static check, identifying selector drift in approximately one second without needing to boot a browser or the application.

The script, approximately 500 lines of Node.js code, cross-references every selector referenced in the test suite against the selectors available in the application's source code. It's designed to integrate with frameworks like Cypress, Playwright, or WebdriverIO, focusing on the naming convention rather than the specific testing tool.

By leveraging the TypeScript compiler, the script parses the codebase to build an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST). This allows it to accurately identify every `cy.getByDataTest(...)` call and its associated string argument, distinguishing them from comments or mere string mentions.

This approach avoids the need for runtime "self-healing" selectors, which can mask underlying issues. Instead, it aims to fail the problematic Pull Request (PR) immediately and deterministically, allowing developers to address the drift proactively.

The convention enforced is that all element access in specs uses a single helper call, like `cy.getByDataTest('...')`, which wraps the framework's native selector. Components, in turn, expose a single test hook, typically `data-test`. This consistency is key to the script's effectiveness.

On its initial run against a fully green test suite, the script successfully identified eight real automation defects, demonstrating its immediate value in catching previously undetected issues and improving test suite reliability.

headline_marked: [[GCC and Clang]] fail to meet C++ standard compliance
headline: GCC and Clang fail to meet C++ standard compliance
summary: Major C++ compilers GCC and Clang have been found non-compliant with the C++ standard, raising concerns for developers.
details: Recent analysis has revealed that two of the most widely used C++ compilers, GNU Compiler Collection (GCC) and Clang, do not fully adhere to the official C++ standard.
This non-compliance means that code which is valid according to the C++ standard might behave unexpectedly or fail to compile correctly on these platforms.
The implications are significant for developers who rely on these compilers for building robust and portable C++ applications.
This issue could lead to subtle bugs, performance regressions, or outright compilation failures, potentially impacting a wide range of software projects.
caption:
Are your C++ projects safe? Major compilers GCC and Clang are reportedly not compliant with the C++ standard.

Recent analysis has revealed that two of the most widely used C++ compilers, GNU Compiler Collection (GCC) and Clang, do not fully adhere to the official C++ standard.

This non-compliance means that code which is valid according to the C++ standard might behave unexpectedly or fail to compile correctly on these platforms.

The implications are significant for developers who rely on these compilers for building robust and portable C++ applications.

This issue could lead to subtle bugs, performance regressions, or outright compilation failures, potentially impacting a wide range of software projects.
